posts.quote: THE SUNDAY PAPER GOT DIVIDED BEFORE BREAKFAST, AND DAD ALWAYS KEPT THE SPORTS PAGE.
posts.caption: Nobody announced it, but the Sunday paper was split up before the coffee finished. Dad took the sports section and the front page, in that order. Mom took the coupons and the TV listings. My brother lay on the living room rug with the funnies spread out like a tablecloth, and I got whatever was left, usually the real estate. If you needed a section somebody else was holding, you waited. Dad would turn a page, snap it straight, and say nothing for twenty minutes. That was about as close as we came to a family meeting.
posts.first: Dad read the obituaries out loud every Sunday, whether we wanted them or not. He would say a name and then add, I knew his brother. By the end of the paper he had known half the county.

posts.quote: THE FAMILY BIBLE HELD THE BIRTHDAYS, THE FUNERAL CARDS, AND A PRESSED FLOWER NOBODY COULD NAME.
posts.caption: It sat on the same shelf for as long as anyone could remember, heavy as a cinder block, with a cracked leather cover. Inside the front pages, in four different handwritings, were the births and weddings and deaths of the whole family. Slipped between the Psalms were funeral cards, a lock of somebody's hair in tissue, and a flower pressed so flat it had turned to paper. Nobody could say whose it was. You were never allowed to carry it around, only to look at it at the table with clean hands. When Grandma finally passed it down, it came with a pencil and an instruction to keep the list going.
posts.first: Our Bible had my great-grandmother's name written in it in careful blue ink, with the date she arrived in this country. I added my own children's names years later, in my own bad handwriting. It felt like signing a very old guest book.

posts.quote: A sandwich cut into triangles meant company was coming.
posts.first: Everyday sandwiches were cut in half, and Mom did not make exceptions. The day she pulled out the good plates and cut the crusts off, we knew somebody was about to knock on the door.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the shoe repair shop)
posts.quote: THE SHOE REPAIR MAN HAD A MOUTHFUL OF TACKS, AND YOUR SHOES CAME BACK WITH NEW HEELS BY FRIDAY.
posts.caption: The shoe repair shop smelled like leather, polish, and hot rubber the second you opened the door. A bell rang over your head and the cobbler never looked up from the machine. He kept a row of tacks in his mouth and somehow still said good morning. You handed over a pair with the heels worn flat on one side and got back a paper ticket torn in half. Friday afternoon they came back with new heels and a shine you could see your face in. A pair of good shoes got resoled three times before anyone thought about buying new ones.
posts.first: Our cobbler was a quiet man on the corner of Main and Third. He kept every customer's ticket stub on a nail, and I never once saw him lose a pair. My father's work boots lasted longer than some of my cars.

posts.quote: THE SCHOOL NURSE / A COT, A THERMOMETER, AND A NOTE TO TAKE HOME
posts.caption: If you felt sick at school, the only way out ran through the nurse's office. It had a narrow cot with a crinkly paper sheet and a glass thermometer that she shook down like a magician. She asked where it hurt, felt your forehead with the back of her hand, and decided in about ten seconds. Real fevers got a phone call home. Everybody else got a cracker, ten minutes on the cot, and a pat on the shoulder back toward the classroom. You could not fool her, but you sure did try.
posts.first: I think I spent half of fourth grade on that cot, mostly before spelling tests. Our nurse never once called my bluff. She would just hand me a cracker and say, ten more minutes, dear.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the shift whistle)
posts.quote: THE SHIFT WHISTLE BLEW AT FOUR, AND THE WHOLE TOWN KNEW EXACTLY WHAT TIME IT WAS.
posts.caption: In a mill town, nobody needed a watch. The whistle blew at four, and you could hear it from the school yard, the grocery, and the back porch. Men came out through the gates in work boots with empty lunch buckets swinging at their sides. Wives set the table a little earlier, and kids on bikes raced down the hill to meet whoever was theirs. By five the whole street smelled like frying onions and machine oil. It was a plain schedule, and everything else in town was built around it.
posts.first: My father worked the second shift for thirty-one years. I could tell the exact minute he turned onto our street by the way the dog stood up. He never once complained about the hours, though his hands told the story for him.

posts.quote: THE PHONE TABLE HAD A BUILT-IN SEAT, A PHONE BOOK, AND A PENCIL ON A STRING.
posts.caption: Every hallway had one. A little wooden table with a padded seat attached, a shelf underneath for the phone book, and a pencil tied to the wall on a string so it could never wander off. The phone sat on top, heavy as a brick, with a cord that reached exactly as far as the table and no farther. You sat down on it to talk, which meant a call was an event you made time for. There was a scrap of paper beside it with every important number written in pencil. Nobody has ever had a better filing system.
posts.first: Ours had a scratch on the seat from my sister's shoe and a smudge of lipstick on the receiver nobody could explain. The numbers on the pad were in three different handwritings. I still remember the plumber's number from that list.

posts.quote: Dad's good hat hung by the front door, and it was the one thing in the house nobody ever borrowed.
posts.first: He wore it to church, funerals, and the bank. It was brushed every Sunday night and never set down on a bed. I still do not know what happened to it.

posts.quote: DRIVER'S EDUCATION / TWO BRAKE PEDALS, ONE TEACHER, AND A VERY QUIET SIXTEEN-YEAR-OLD
posts.caption: The driver's ed car had a second brake pedal on the passenger side, and the teacher's foot never left it. You pulled out of the school lot at about eight miles an hour while he said gently, a little more gas. Three of you rode along, taking turns, and the two in the back seat held on like it was a roller coaster. He never raised his voice, which somehow made it worse. By the end of the semester you could parallel park between two cones, and he looked ten years older.
posts.first: Mine was a Mr. Halvorsen who wore the same brown windbreaker every day. He once said very calmly, you may want to look at the curb. I did, and we both survived.

posts.quote: THE WINDOW FAN PULLED IN THE NIGHT AIR, AND EVERYBODY SLEPT TO ITS HUM.
posts.caption: On the hottest nights of July, the whole house depended on one box fan in the window. Dad set it facing in, and it pulled the cooler air across the yard and through every room. You lay on top of the sheet with your arms flung out and listened to it hum. The curtains breathed in and out. Somewhere a screen door slapped, and far off a train went through. Nobody could sleep until the fan went on, and once it did, nobody remembered falling asleep.
posts.first: Ours had a rattle in the left blade that I can still hear if I think about it. We tied a strip of cloth to the grille to see which way the air was moving. My brother swore it made him dream about trains.
